title: Beyond Independent Manipulation: Individual Fairness-aware Strategic Classification with Peer Imitation

problem.claim: Individual-fairness requirements make agents' strategic manipulation interdependent because an agent's preferred manipulation depends on neighborhood outcomes.

gap.claim: Classical strategic-classification formulations and independent-response models do not accurately characterize manipulation in fairness-aware settings requiring individual fairness.

contributions.claim: Introduces individual fairness-aware strategic classification (IFSC), a framework for modeling peer-driven manipulation under individual fairness.
Represents manipulation as similarity-guided imitation of observable accepted peers and trains classifiers on the resulting post-manipulation distributions.
Uses stochastic perturbations during manipulation simulation to support robust learning under uncertainty in peer observability.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report improved individual-fairness consistency and reduced imitation-induced distortions.

narrative_sequence.summary: Strategic classification studies feature manipulation to obtain favorable predictive decisions.

Existing fairness-aware approaches emphasize group fairness and independent agent responses, but individual fairness creates interdependent manipulation and exposes a mismatch with classical formulations.
IFSC models peer-driven imitation toward visible accepted peers and learns under post-manipulation distributions.
The framework simulates uncertainty in peer observability with stochastic perturbations, and experiments report improved fairness consistency and mitigated distortions.

source_observation.claim: When fairness depends on similarity across individuals, one agent's manipulation objective can depend on nearby peers' outcomes.

interpretation.claim: Strategic-response models may need to represent social or neighborhood dependence instead of treating agents as independent optimizers.

application.claim: For fairness-aware deployment settings with observable peer outcomes, evaluate models under imitation or other interdependent response mechanisms.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that peer imitation is present or dominant in every application setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not detail the individual-fairness definition, imitation dynamics, or perturbation process.
